questions.question: Zamani Ltd's sales are R4 200 000 and cost of sales R2 800 000. Other operating income is R100 000, operating expenses R880 000, interest income R20 000, interest expense R60 000, and the tax rate 27 percent. Build the statement of comprehensive income down to net profit after tax, and confirm the mark-up on cost.
questions.expected_answer: Gross profit is R4 200 000 less R2 800 000, which is R1 400 000 — a mark-up on cost of 1 400 000 over 2 800 000, 50 percent. Add other operating income of R100 000 for gross operating income of R1 500 000, deduct operating expenses of R880 000 for an operating profit of R620 000. Add interest income of R20 000 to reach R640 000, deduct interest expense of R60 000 for net profit before tax of R580 000. Income tax at 27 percent is R156 600, leaving net profit after tax of R423 400. Dividends never appear among the expenses — they are a distribution of profit shown in the retained income note. The three profit levels each measure a different skill: gross profit tests buying and pricing, operating profit tests running the operation, and net profit tests the effect of financing.

questions.question: Using net profit after tax of R423 400, an interim dividend of R130 000 paid in October, a final dividend of R150 000 declared on the last day, and opening retained income of R256 600, prepare the retained income note. Then state where the final dividend and the outstanding SARS balance of R38 600 appear on the statement of financial position, and why.
questions.expected_answer: The retained income note: opening balance R256 600, plus net profit after tax R423 400, less dividends of R280 000 — the interim dividend of R130 000 and the final dividend of R150 000 — leaving a closing balance of R400 000, which appears in shareholders' equity next to ordinary share capital. The final dividend of R150 000 appears under current liabilities as Shareholders for Dividends, because it was declared on the last day of the year and only becomes payable early in the new year — declaration creates the debt, payment settles it. The SARS balance of R38 600 also sits under current liabilities: the year's tax charge was R156 600 against provisional payments of R118 000, so R38 600 is still owed to SARS. Had the provisional payments exceeded the charge, the balance would cross the statement and appear as a current asset — a refund due — so the account must be read, never assumed.

questions.question: Zamani Ltd's net profit before tax is R580 000, depreciation R210 000 and interest expense R60 000. Inventories rose R50 000, receivables rose R30 000 and payables rose R42 000. Interest paid was R60 000, income tax paid R143 000 and dividends paid R250 000. Investing used R550 000 and financing produced R160 000. Opening cash was R231 000. Complete the cash flow statement and explain what the closing figure must equal.
questions.expected_answer: Start with net profit before tax of R580 000 and add back the non-cash and separately-disclosed items: depreciation of R210 000 and interest expense of R60 000, giving R850 000 before working capital changes. The working capital movements: inventories up R50 000 is cash out, receivables up R30 000 is cash out, payables up R42 000 is cash in — cash generated from operations is R812 000. Deduct the actual payments: interest paid R60 000, income tax paid R143 000, dividends paid R250 000 — net cash from operating activities R359 000. Combine the three sections: R359 000 in from operations, R550 000 out for investing, R160 000 in from financing — a net decrease of R31 000. Opening cash of R231 000 less R31 000 gives closing cash of R200 000, which must equal the cash and cash equivalents figure in current assets on the statement of financial position. When the statement lands exactly on that figure, the whole chain is proven; when it does not, there is an error to find.
